pel3: The pelvic floor muscles support the bladder and bowel; when they are strong, leaking when you cough, sneeze or lift something becomes less likely. These exercises are for women and men. pel58: Squeeze your pelvic floor muscles just before and during coughing, sneezing, laughing or lifting something heavy. This habit helps reduce or prevent leaks. Once you can comfortably do 10 squeezes of 10 seconds, also try the exercises standing, squatting or stepping forward into a lunge.
pel59: Who are pelvic floor exercises for?
pel60: Women and men. They are most often recommended for leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or laughing, a frequent and sudden urge to go to the toilet, after childbirth and after prostate surgery. If you have had surgery, a birth or treatment, your team may have specific advice for you; follow that first.
pel62: Yes. In a Cochrane review of 31 randomised trials and 1,817 women, 56% of women with leakage on coughing and exertion who did pelvic floor exercises reported being cured, compared with 6% of those who did not exercise. For cure or marked improvement, the figures were 74% versus 11%. The review included only women, and most trials followed people up for less than a year.
pel63: When will I notice a difference?
pel64: Muscles take time to strengthen: practise regularly for at least 3 months. If at first you can only hold for a few seconds or manage a few repetitions, that’s fine; keep going and build up gradually.
pel65: How do I know I’m using the right muscles?
pel66: Place a hand on the area between your anus and genitals (the perineum): when you squeeze, it should lift up away from your hand. Don’t clench your buttocks, thighs or jaw, don’t hold your breath and don’t pull your tummy in.
